base_method_text.title:
Efficient coding of natural scene statistics predicts discrimination
  thresholds for grayscale textures
base_method_text.summary:
Previously, in (Hermundstad et al., 2014), we showed that when sampling is
limiting, the efficient coding principle leads to a "variance is salience"
hypothesis, and that this hypothesis accounts for visual sensitivity to binary
image statistics. Here, using extensive new psychophysical data and image
analysis, we show that this hypothesis accounts for visual sensitivity to a
large set of grayscale image statistics at a striking level of detail, and also
identify the limits of the prediction. We define a 66-dimensional space of
local grayscale light-intensity correlations, and measure the relevance of each
direction to natural scenes. The "variance is salience" hypothesis predicts
that two-point correlations are most salient, and predicts their relative
salience. We tested these predictions in a texture-segregation task using
un-natural, synthetic textures. As predicted, correlations beyond second order
are not salient, and predicted thresholds for over 300 second-order
correlations match psychophysical thresholds closely (median fractional error
<0.13).
base_method_text.main_contributions: The study investigates the relationship between natural scene statistics and visual perception by testing the "variance is salience" hypothesis for grayscale textures. It defines a 66-dimensional space of local grayscale light-intensity correlations and demonstrates that human sensitivity to second-order correlations closely matches predictions derived from natural image statistics. The research also identifies invariances in psychophysical thresholds that reflect symmetries in natural images.
base_method_text.methodology: The methodology involves analyzing natural images to quantify the variance of different grayscale texture correlations. Psychophysical experiments are conducted using a texture-segregation task with synthetic textures. Observers report the location of textured strips, and detection thresholds are measured. The predicted thresholds based on natural image statistics are compared with the psychophysical thresholds.
base_method_text.experimental_setup: The UPenn Natural Image Database and van Hateren database are used for natural image analysis. Synthetic grayscale textures with three luminance levels (black, gray, light) are generated using a Markov process to control the correlations. A four-alternative forced-choice paradigm is used in the psychophysical experiments, and thresholds are determined by fitting a Weibull function to the subject's performance.
base_method_text.limitations: The study acknowledges that the efficient-coding model has limitations, as indicated by systematic discrepancies between natural-image predictions and measured thresholds, particularly underestimation in simple planes and overestimation in mixed planes. The preprocessing pipeline reduces the dark-light asymmetry present in natural images, potentially affecting the results. The model also assumes linearity, which may not fully capture the complexities of visual processing.
base_method_text.future_research_directions: Future research directions include exploring the limits of texture adaptation by considering the cost-benefit trade-offs of efficiently coding increasingly complex environmental statistics. The authors suggest investigating non-linear transformations of natural-image variances to improve the model's accuracy. Generalizing the construction to larger numbers of gray levels and correlations over greater distances is also mentioned.

add_method_texts.title:
Learning High-Frequency Functions Made Easy with Sinusoidal Positional
  Encoding
add_method_texts.summary:
Fourier features based positional encoding (PE) is commonly used in machine
learning tasks that involve learning high-frequency features from
low-dimensional inputs, such as 3D view synthesis and time series regression
with neural tangent kernels. Despite their effectiveness, existing PEs require
manual, empirical adjustment of crucial hyperparameters, specifically the
Fourier features, tailored to each unique task. Further, PEs face challenges in
efficiently learning high-frequency functions, particularly in tasks with
limited data. In this paper, we introduce sinusoidal PE (SPE), designed to
efficiently learn adaptive frequency features closely aligned with the true
underlying function. Our experiments demonstrate that SPE, without
hyperparameter tuning, consistently achieves enhanced fidelity and faster
training across various tasks, including 3D view synthesis, Text-to-Speech
generation, and 1D regression. SPE is implemented as a direct replacement for
existing PEs. Its plug-and-play nature lets numerous tasks easily adopt and
benefit from SPE.
add_method_texts.main_contributions: The paper introduces Sinusoidal Positional Encoding (SPE), a novel positional encoding method that learns adaptive frequency features aligned with the underlying function. It addresses the limitations of existing positional encodings (PEs) that require manual hyperparameter tuning and struggle with learning high-frequency functions, especially with limited data. The key finding is that SPE consistently achieves enhanced fidelity and faster training across various tasks without hyperparameter tuning.
add_method_texts.methodology: SPE augments PE with periodic activation functions, making the number and frequencies of Fourier series trainable and adaptive to inputs. It uses a sinusoidal activation function after the traditional positional encoding to allow the network to learn the optimal frequency features. The method can be implemented as a direct replacement for existing PEs.
add_method_texts.experimental_setup: The paper evaluates SPE on 3D view synthesis (NeRF), Text-to-Speech generation (FastSpeech), and 1D regression with neural tangent kernel (NTK). For NeRF, the Blender dataset is used. Performance is measured using PSNR, SSIM, Wavelet Decomposition Power Ratio (WDPR), and Relative Wasserstein Distance Error (RWDE).
add_method_texts.limitations: The paper does not explicitly discuss limitations of the SPE method itself. However, it implicitly acknowledges that the effectiveness of SPE, like other neural network techniques, depends on the architecture of the MLP and the number of parameters.
add_method_texts.future_research_directions: The paper suggests potential for exploring other periodic activation functions and network architectures to further enhance the performance of SPE. Also, the use of GANs to further refine the results from SPE-enhanced NeRF models are worth further investigation.

new_method:
Below is an illustrative example of a new method—drawing on both the Base Method and an “Add Method” approach—that aims to address several of the Base Method’s recognized limitations.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
STEP 3: A NEW METHOD INSPIRED BY THE BASE METHOD AND SINUSOIDAL PE
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1. Core Idea.  
   We propose integrating high-frequency sinusoidal encoding into the “variance is salience” framework to create a nonlinear texture-analysis model. This approach retains the Base Method’s physiological grounding (i.e., building on natural scene statistics and variance-based salience) but augments it with an adaptive sinusoidal mechanism to better capture higher-order correlations and preserve relevant dark-light asymmetries.

2. Overview of the Pipeline.  
   a) Enhanced Data Preparation.  
      • Preserve Asymmetry. Instead of discarding or normalizing away dark-light imbalances, we adopt an asymmetry-preserving preprocessing step. For instance, we maintain separate grayscale bands (darker vs. lighter patches) and augment them with mild contrast modifications, ensuring the model sees a more representative sample of real-world luminance extremes.  
      • Multi-Scale Patches. Combine low-, mid-, and high-resolution patches so that the resulting dataset includes a spectrum of texture frequencies.

   b) Sinusoidal Encoding Module.  
      • Position + Luminance Embedding. Each pixel or patch is encoded using both its spatial position (e.g., patch coordinates) and local luminance. The luminance is cast through a trainable sinusoidal layer that automatically learns the dominant frequency components in the texture.  
      • Adaptive Frequency. Instead of manually selecting the frequencies as in standard Fourier features, the sinusoidal layer learns them end-to-end, thereby identifying the “critical” frequency bands that drive salience in nature-inspired textures.

   c) Nonlinear Salience Network.  
      • Network Architecture. A small MLP or convolutional backbone (depending on the image dimensions) receives the sinusoidally encoded representations of texture patches.  
      • Variance-Weighted Output. The final layer of the network is regularized to preserve the “variance is salience” intuition: learned weights emphasize dimensions whose frequency variance is consistently high in natural images. This helps the model to maintain alignment with the Base Method’s principle that strongly varying correlations typically indicate salient changes.  
      • Psychophysical Threshold Estimator. The network outputs a salience profile for each patch correlation; these are then translated into predicted detection thresholds via a calibration curve, fit in a manner similar to how the Base Method derived psychophysical thresholds.

3. Anticipated Benefits.  
   • Richer Representation of Correlations. By using sinusoidal encodings, the method captures higher-order and high-frequency correlations that might be missed by a purely linear variance-based model, particularly in cases where texture statistics are more complex than simple second-order relationships.  
   • Automatic Frequency Selection. Unlike traditional Fourier-based positional encodings, there is no need to predefine specific frequencies. The adaptive sinusoidal module finds a suitable representation for a variety of texture complexities.  
   • Improved Alignment with Actual Vision. Preserving dark-light asymmetry and incorporating learnable high-frequency features provide a more accurate reflection of natural images and visual sensitivities, thereby mitigating the under- and over-estimation of thresholds observed in the Base Method.

4. Experimental Validation.  
   • Synthetic Texture Segregation Tests. Perform the same forced-choice experiments as in the Base Method but now with textures generated at varying luminance levels and frequency spectrums. Compare predicted thresholds from the new network vs. measured psychophysical data.  
   • Natural Image Generalization. Evaluate the model’s ability to predict salience in genuine natural scenes, including scenes with strong contrast transitions, diverse lighting, and varied local textures.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

In sum, this new approach integrates the Base Method’s reliance on natural-image variances with a sinusoidal embedding module that adaptively learns high-frequency correlations important for visual discrimination. By preserving dark-light asymmetries and leveraging the flexibility of trainable sinusoidal layers, the method aspires to more faithfully mirror human sensitivity to grayscale textures.
verification_policy:
Below is an outline of three concrete experiments we can implement in Python to evaluate and demonstrate the superiority of the New Method:

──────────────────────────────
1. Synthetic Texture Segregation Test

• Aim: To compare the salience predictions produced by the Base Method versus our new sinusoidally encoded framework.

• Plan:
  – Generate a suite of synthetic textures having controlled levels of variance and deliberate dark–light imbalances. We can use libraries like numpy and OpenCV to create grayscale textures at various luminance levels.
  – Introduce multi-scale patches into the pipeline by downsampling/upscaling patches to simulate low, mid, and high-resolution segments.
  – Process these textures through both implementations: (a) the Base Method and (b) the New Method. For (b), include the adaptive sinusoidal encoding module.
  – For each synthetic texture, obtain predicted salience profiles and compare them to a set of ground‐truth psychophysical thresholds (simulated or drawn from prior experiments).
  – Analyze discrepancies in threshold predictions, looking for improved alignment with human-like responses in the New Method.

• Implementation: All components—from texture generation to salience profile computation—can be scripted in Python using numpy for computations, OpenCV for image manipulation, and PyTorch (or TensorFlow) for the small MLP/convolutional network.

──────────────────────────────
2. Adaptive Frequency Visualization and Analysis

• Aim: To explicitly validate that the sinusoidal layer in the New Method learns meaningful frequency components, thereby capturing higher-order correlations that the Base Method might miss.

• Plan:
  – Train the New Method on a controlled dataset of textures with known high-frequency content (for instance, textures generated with defined sinusoidal frequencies).
  – Extract and record the learned frequency parameters (or weights from the sinusoidal embedding module) after training.
  – Plot the distribution of these frequencies and overlay them with the actual frequencies embedded in the synthetic textures.
  – In parallel, run a baseline experiment using fixed Fourier features (as used in classic encoding schemes) to visualize any disparities in frequency selection.
  – Correlate the differences between learned and fixed frequencies with improvements in salience prediction accuracy.

• Implementation: Python packages such as matplotlib/seaborn for visualization and numpy for numerical analysis ensure that we can both plot the learned weights and implement controlled comparisons. PyTorch’s autograd functionality will assist in extracting parameters from the network.

──────────────────────────────
3. Natural Image Generalization Test

• Aim: To test whether the New Method’s benefits extend to real-world scenes and complex textures beyond synthetic data.

• Plan:
  – Collect or use an existing dataset of natural images (e.g., from the BSDS500 or another public dataset) that display a range of lighting extremes and texture contrasts.
  – Preprocess these images using the asymmetry-preserving and multi-scale patch extraction pipeline. This step will maintain distinct dark/light neighborhood information.
  – Pass the preprocessed images through both the Base and New Methods to generate salience maps or predicted detection thresholds.
  – Evaluate the performance by comparing these predictions to established benchmarks or, if available, psychophysical measurement data that indicate human sensitivity to certain regions in natural images.
  – Perform quantitative analysis such as computing correlation coefficients or ROC curves, and visualize qualitative differences (for instance, by overlaying salience maps on images).

• Implementation: Python’s image processing libraries (OpenCV, PIL) and deep learning frameworks (PyTorch) will be used for data handling and model inference. Evaluation metrics can be computed with sklearn or custom routines as appropriate.

──────────────────────────────
Summary

These three experiments together verify that:
– The New Method produces more accurate salience predictions on controlled synthetic textures;
– Its adaptive sinusoidal encoding learns frequency components that correspond to the actual underlying texture patterns;
– These advantages persist when processing real natural images, hence demonstrating its superiority over the Base Method.

All experiments are realistic and fully implementable in Python, utilizing standard libraries such as numpy, OpenCV, PyTorch, and matplotlib.
experiment_details:
Below is a detailed description of three experiments that we can implement in Python using PyTorch (along with supporting libraries such as numpy, OpenCV, matplotlib, and scikit‐learn) to verify the superiority of the New Method over the Base Method. Each experiment is designed to be as close as possible to the original experimental information while ensuring that results are statistically reliable, and they avoid excessive overlap by targeting distinct aspects of performance. You can combine several verification policies in one experiment where appropriate.

──────────────────────────────
Experiment 1. Synthetic Texture Segregation Test

Aim:
• Compare the salience predictions produced by the Base Method versus the New Method using synthetic textures.
• Validate the improvement in predicting psychophysical thresholds (simulated ground‐truth) with multi-scale patch representations.

Plan:
1. Texture Generation:
   • Use numpy and OpenCV to generate grayscale textures with controlled luminance.
   • Introduce systematic dark–light imbalances by modulating intensity levels.
   • Create multi‐scale patches by downsampling/upscaling portions of the image to simulate low, mid, and high resolutions.

2. Model Pipeline:
   • Implement a Base Method pipeline that directly feeds the multi-scale patches into a network (e.g., a small convolutional or MLP network defined in PyTorch).
   • Implement the New Method pipeline that includes the novel adaptive sinusoidal encoding module as the first layer.
   • Ensure that both pipelines share the same overall architecture for the remainder of the network so that the only difference is the encoding layer.

3. Salience Prediction and Evaluation:
   • For each synthetic texture, process the images through both pipelines and obtain salience profiles (or computed detection thresholds).
   • Compare these outputs against simulated ground‐truth psychophysical thresholds.
   • Quantitatively evaluate the discrepancy (e.g., using mean absolute error or correlation coefficients) and qualitatively analyze the output profiles.
   • Use statistical tests (e.g., paired t-test) across multiple textures to confirm that improvements are statistically significant.

Implementation Example (Code Sample):

------------------------------------------------------------
import numpy as np
import cv2
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.optim as optim
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Define helper function to generate synthetic texture
def generate_texture(width, height, imbalance_factor=0.2):
    """Generate a synthetic grayscale texture with a controlled dark/light imbalance."""
    base_texture = np.random.rand(height, width) * 255
    # Artificially adjust a region to simulate an imbalance 
    cv2.rectangle(base_texture, (width//4, height//4), (width//2, height//2),
                  int(255 * (1 - imbalance_factor)), -1)  # dark patch
    return base_texture.astype(np.uint8)

# Multi-scale patch extraction (using OpenCV for resizing)
def extract_multiscale_patches(img, scales=[1.0, 0.5, 0.25]):
    patches = []
    for s in scales:
        resized = cv2.resize(img, (0, 0), fx=s, fy=s, interpolation=cv2.INTER_LINEAR)
        patches.append(resized)
    return patches

# Define the Base Method: simple CNN or MLP
class BaseMethod(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super(BaseMethod, self).__init__()
        self.conv = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(1, 8, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1)
        )
        self.fc = nn.Linear(8, 1)
        
    def forward(self, x):
        out = self.conv(x)
        out = out.view(out.size(0), -1)
        return self.fc(out)

# Define the New Method with the sinusoidal encoding layer
class SinusoidalEncoding(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_channels, embedding_size):
        super(SinusoidalEncoding, self).__init__()
        # Learnable frequencies and phase offsets
        self.freqs = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(in_channels, embedding_size))
        self.phases = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(in_channels, embedding_size))
        
    def forward(self, x):
        # x is assumed to be a feature map, apply sinusoidal transform element-wise
        # For simplicity, assume x shape: batch x channels x H x W, here we transform per-channel
        # Expand dimensions to apply sinusoid on an additional embedding dimension
        x_expanded = x.unsqueeze(-1)  # shape: batch x channels x H x W x 1
        encoded = torch.sin(x_expanded * self.freqs + self.phases)
        # Aggregate along the embedding dimension
        encoded = torch.mean(encoded, dim=-1)
        return encoded

class NewMethod(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, embedding_size=10):
        super(NewMethod, self).__init__()
        # Start with sinusoidal encoding layer (assuming grayscale input, so 1 channel)
        self.sinusoid = SinusoidalEncoding(in_channels=1, embedding_size=embedding_size)
        # Follow with similar CNN layers as BaseMethod
        self.conv = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(1, 8, kernel_size=3, padding=1),  # note: after encoding, channel count remains same
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1)
        )
        self.fc = nn.Linear(8, 1)
        
    def forward(self, x):
        x_encoded = self.sinusoid(x)
        out = self.conv(x_encoded)
        out = out.view(out.size(0), -1)
        return self.fc(out)

# Example experiment loop
device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
base_model = BaseMethod().to(device)
new_model = NewMethod(embedding_size=10).to(device)

criterion = nn.MSELoss()
optimizer_new = optim.Adam(new_model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
optimizer_base = optim.Adam(base_model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)

# Generate a batch of synthetic textures
batch_size = 10
textures = []
for _ in range(batch_size):
    tex = generate_texture(128, 128, imbalance_factor=0.3)
    textures.append(tex)
    
# For simplicity, assume ground truth threshold is computed as some function of average intensity
ground_truth = [np.mean(tex)/255.0 for tex in textures]

# Prepare dataset (simple example without dataloaders)
def prepare_tensor(image):
    # Normalize and add channel and batch dimension: (1, H, W)
    tensor = torch.tensor(image, dtype=torch.float32).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) / 255.0
    return tensor.to(device)

# Train or evaluate on the synthetic textures
base_outputs = []
new_outputs = []
for img, gt in zip(textures, ground_truth):
    tensor_in = prepare_tensor(img)
    
    # Forward with Base Method
    pred_base = base_model(tensor_in)
    base_outputs.append(pred_base.item())
    
    # Forward with New Method
    pred_new = new_model(tensor_in)
    new_outputs.append(pred_new.item())

print("Base Method Predictions:", base_outputs)
print("New Method Predictions:", new_outputs)

# Here, one would compute error metrics against the ground_truth and visualize differences.
------------------------------------------------------------

Key Measurements:
• Error metrics (e.g., mean absolute error) between predicted thresholds and ground truth.
• Statistical tests (e.g., paired t-tests) comparing performance across textures.
• Visual overlay of salience profiles on synthetic textures using matplotlib.

──────────────────────────────
Experiment 2. Adaptive Frequency Visualization and Analysis

Aim:
• Validate that the sinusoidal layer in the New Method learns meaningful frequency components.
• Compare learned frequency parameters to fixed Fourier features, showing that the adaptive method better captures high-frequency content.

Plan:
1. Data Preparation:
   • Generate a controlled dataset of synthetic textures with known high-frequency content. For example, create textures containing sine waves of specified frequencies.
   
2. Training:
   • Train the New Method using the same architecture as above, but on this controlled dataset.
   • In parallel, set up a baseline network using fixed Fourier feature encoding without learnable parameters.
   
3. Parameter Extraction and Visualization:
   • After training, extract the learned frequency parameters (self.freqs and self.phases) from the New Method.
   • Plot histograms/distributions of these frequencies using matplotlib or seaborn.
   • Overlay the distribution of frequencies present in the synthetic textures to inspect alignment.
   • Compare this to the baseline “fixed” Fourier features to highlight differences.

Implementation Example (Code Snippet):

------------------------------------------------------------
# Assume we have a function to generate sine textures with a given frequency:
def generate_sine_texture(width, height, frequency):
    x = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi * frequency, width)
    sine_row = (np.sin(x) * 0.5 + 0.5) * 255
    texture = np.tile(sine_row, (height, 1))
    return texture.astype(np.uint8)

# Create a controlled dataset with different known frequencies
frequencies = [3, 5, 7, 10]
sine_textures = [generate_sine_texture(128, 128, f) for f in frequencies]

# Training loop for the New Method on sine textures:
new_model.train()
for epoch in range(20):  # a short training loop for demonstration
    epoch_loss = 0
    for texture in sine_textures:
        tensor_in = prepare_tensor(texture)
        # For synthetic ground truth, assume the threshold is proportional to the frequency
        gt_threshold = torch.tensor([[np.mean(texture)/255.0 + 0.1 * np.log(f+1)]], device=device)
        
        optimizer_new.zero_grad()
        pred = new_model(tensor_in)
        loss = criterion(pred, gt_threshold)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer_new.step()
        epoch_loss += loss.item()
    print(f"Epoch {epoch+1}, Loss: {epoch_loss/len(sine_textures)}")

# After training, extract and visualize frequency parameters:
learned_freqs = new_model.sinusoid.freqs.data.cpu().numpy()
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
plt.hist(learned_freqs.flatten(), bins=20, alpha=0.7, label="Learned Frequencies")
plt.xlabel("Frequency Value")
plt.ylabel("Count")
plt.title("Distribution of Learned Sinusoidal Frequencies")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

# For comparison, plot fixed Fourier frequencies (here we assume a fixed initialization)
fixed_fourier_freqs = np.linspace(0, 10, num=learned_freqs.size).reshape(learned_freqs.shape)
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
plt.hist(fixed_fourier_freqs.flatten(), bins=20, alpha=0.7, color='green', label="Fixed Fourier Frequencies")
plt.xlabel("Frequency Value")
plt.ylabel("Count")
plt.title("Distribution of Fixed Fourier Frequencies")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
------------------------------------------------------------

Key Measurements:
• Visual overlays comparing the learned frequency distributions with the sine frequencies embedded in the textures.
• Quantitative correlation metrics that relate learned frequency parameters to the known input frequencies.
• Comparison plots against a fixed Fourier encoding scheme.

──────────────────────────────
Experiment 3. Natural Image Generalization Test

Aim:
• Evaluate whether the performance gains in synthetic texture experiments extend to real-world textures and scenes.
• Generate salience maps from both the Base and New Methods on natural images and compare these to established benchmarks or psychophysical data.

Plan:
1. Data Collection:
   • Use an existing public dataset (for example, BSDS500) containing natural images with diverse textures and lighting conditions.
   
2. Preprocessing:
   • Preprocess images using OpenCV or PIL.
   • Use an asymmetry-preserving pipeline to extract multi-scale patches that respect local dark/light neighborhood differences.
   • Normalize the images appropriately for network input.
   
3. Model Inference and Evaluation:
   • Process the images through both the Base and New Method pipelines to obtain salience maps or threshold predictions.
   • Compare the predicted salience maps quantitatively (using correlation coefficients, ROC curves, etc.) against available human sensitivity data or benchmarks.
   • Qualitatively overlay the resulting salience maps on the natural images to visually inspect improvements.
   
4. Statistical Analysis:
   • Aggregate error measures from all images and perform statistical tests to ensure that improvements with the New Method are robust.

Implementation Example (Code Snippet):

------------------------------------------------------------
from torchvision import transforms
from PIL import Image
import glob

# Assume a directory "BSDS500_images" with natural image files
image_paths = glob.glob("BSDS500_images/*.jpg")
if len(image_paths) == 0:
    print("No images found. Please ensure the dataset is available.")

# Define preprocessing transformation
preprocess = transforms.Compose([
    transforms.Resize((128, 128)),
    transforms.ToTensor()  # scales images to [0, 1] and converts to tensor
])

# Set models to evaluation mode:
base_model.eval()
new_model.eval()

def get_salience_map(model, image_tensor):
    # For demonstration, assume the network returns a scalar threshold,
    # but this can be extended to a full spatial salience map if necessary.
    with torch.no_grad():
        output = model(image_tensor.unsqueeze(0))  # add batch dimension
    return output.item()

results = []
for path in image_paths:
    image = Image.open(path).convert("L")  # convert to grayscale
    tensor_img = preprocess(image).unsqueeze(0).to(device)  # add batch dimension
    
    # Optionally, extract multi-scale patches and combine them (this part can be customized)
    # For simplicity, we use the whole image here.
    
    salience_base = get_salience_map(base_model, tensor_img[0])
    salience_new = get_salience_map(new_model, tensor_img[0])
    
    results.append((path, salience_base, salience_new))
    # Visualize overlay (if salience maps are full spatial maps, here we assume scalar values)
    print(f"Image: {path}")
    print(f"Base Method Salience: {salience_base:.4f} vs New Method Salience: {salience_new:.4f}")

# After collecting predictions, one can compute metrics across images:
base_preds = [res[1] for res in results]
new_preds = [res[2] for res in results]
# If ground truth exists, compute correlation or ROC curves using sklearn
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score
# Assuming we have ground_truth_values for each image (this is a placeholder)
# ground_truth_values = [...]
# For demonstration, we print out the predictions.
print("Evaluation on natural images completed.")
------------------------------------------------------------

Key Measurements:
• Quantitative measures such as correlation coefficients between model predictions and ground truth.
• ROC curves, precision-recall curves, or area under the curve (AUC) based on any available psychophysical benchmark data.
• Visual overlays of salience maps to capture qualitative differences.
• Comparison of how well each method handles localized dark/light contrasts in complex, natural scenes.

──────────────────────────────
Summary

Together, these experiments will:
• Demonstrate that the New Method produces more accurate salience predictions on synthetic textures by better aligning with psychophysical thresholds (Experiment 1).
• Show that the sinusoidal encoding layer learns meaningful frequency components that correspond to the underlying texture patterns, outperforming fixed Fourier encodings (Experiment 2).
• Validate that the New Method generalizes to natural images, maintaining its advantages on real-world scenes with complex textures and lighting conditions (Experiment 3).

Each experiment uses realistic, fully implementable Python code utilizing standard libraries and frameworks (PyTorch, numpy, OpenCV, matplotlib, and sklearn) to ensure reproducibility and reliability. Researchers can adjust parameters (such as network architectures, learning rates, and training epochs) to suit specific evaluation settings, while the overall pipeline adheres closely to the experimental setups in the original research.
experiment_code:
Below is a complete Python script implementing the three experiments as described. In this implementation we use PyTorch (for both models and training loops), numpy, OpenCV, matplotlib, seaborn, scikit‐learn (for statistical tests) and torchvision (for natural image preprocessing). To conform with the requirements, all plots are saved as PDF files using the prescribed naming format.

You can save the code below in a Python file (for example, experiment_run.py) and run it. A test function is provided at the end that runs a minimal version of each experiment to verify execution.

------------------------------------------------------------
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Necessary libraries:
 • numpy
 • opencv-python
 • torch
 • torchvision
 • matplotlib
 • seaborn
 • scikit-learn
 • scipy
"""

import numpy as np
import cv2
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.optim as optim
from torchvision import transforms
from PIL import Image
import glob
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score
from scipy.stats import ttest_rel
import os

# Set random seed for reproducibility
np.random.seed(42)
torch.manual_seed(42)

###############################
# Helper Functions for Data Generation
###############################
def generate_texture(width, height, imbalance_factor=0.2):
    """
    Generate a synthetic grayscale texture with controlled dark/light imbalance.
    A rectangular (darker) region is inserted into the random texture.
    """
    base_texture = np.random.rand(height, width) * 255
    # Create a dark patch in the center to simulate imbalance
    cv2.rectangle(base_texture, (width//4, height//4), (width//2, height//2),
                  int(255 * (1 - imbalance_factor)), -1)
    return base_texture.astype(np.uint8)

def extract_multiscale_patches(img, scales=[1.0, 0.5, 0.25]):
    """
    Extract multi-scale patches from an image using different scaling factors.
    """
    patches = []
    for s in scales:
        resized = cv2.resize(img, (0, 0), fx=s, fy=s, interpolation=cv2.INTER_LINEAR)
        patches.append(resized)
    return patches

def generate_sine_texture(width, height, frequency):
    """
    Generate a sine texture (sinusoidal pattern) with a specified frequency.
    """
    x = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi * frequency, width)
    sine_row = (np.sin(x) * 0.5 + 0.5) * 255
    texture = np.tile(sine_row, (height, 1))
    return texture.astype(np.uint8)

def prepare_tensor(image):
    """
    Convert image (numpy.ndarray) to tensor, normalize, and add channel and batch dimensions.
    Assumes grayscale image.
    """
    tensor = torch.tensor(image, dtype=torch.float32).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) / 255.0
    return tensor

###############################
# Model Definitions
###############################
class BaseMethod(nn.Module):
    """
    Base Method:
    A simple CNN that processes an image and outputs a single scalar (e.g., salience threshold).
    """
    def __init__(self):
        super(BaseMethod, self).__init__()
        self.conv = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(1, 8, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1)
        )
        self.fc = nn.Linear(8, 1)
        
    def forward(self, x):
        out = self.conv(x)
        out = out.view(out.size(0), -1)
        return self.fc(out)

class SinusoidalEncoding(nn.Module):
    """
    Adaptive sinusoidal encoding layer.
    Uses learnable frequency and phase parameters.
    """
    def __init__(self, in_channels, embedding_size):
        super(SinusoidalEncoding, self).__init__()
        self.freqs = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(in_channels, embedding_size))
        self.phases = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(in_channels, embedding_size))
        
    def forward(self, x):
        # x shape: batch x channels x H x W
        # Add an embedding dimension before applying sinusoid
        x_expanded = x.unsqueeze(-1)  # shape: batch x channels x H x W x 1
        # Broadcasting freq and phase to x’s shape (using unsqueeze for proper dimensions)
        encoded = torch.sin(x_expanded * self.freqs.view(1, -1, 1, 1, self.freqs.shape[-1]) 
                              + self.phases.view(1, -1, 1, 1, self.phases.shape[-1]))
        # Aggregate along the embedding dimension (mean)
        encoded = torch.mean(encoded, dim=-1)
        return encoded

class NewMethod(nn.Module):
    """
    New Method:
    Starts with the sinusoidal encoding layer followed by similar CNN layers as BaseMethod.
    """
    def __init__(self, embedding_size=10):
        super(NewMethod, self).__init__()
        self.sinusoid = SinusoidalEncoding(in_channels=1, embedding_size=embedding_size)
        self.conv = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(1, 8, kernel_size=3, padding=1),  # after encoding channels remain the same
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1)
        )
        self.fc = nn.Linear(8, 1)
        
    def forward(self, x):
        x_encoded = self.sinusoid(x)
        out = self.conv(x_encoded)
        out = out.view(out.size(0), -1)
        return self.fc(out)

# Experiment 1: Synthetic Texture Segregation Test
###############################
def experiment1_synthetic_texture_test(device):
    print("Running Experiment 1: Synthetic Texture Segregation Test")
    # Instantiate both models and move them to the device
    base_model = BaseMethod().to(device)
    new_model = NewMethod(embedding_size=10).to(device)
    
    # Define error criterion and optimizers (if training were required)
    criterion = nn.MSELoss()
    optimizer_base = optim.Adam(base_model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
    optimizer_new = optim.Adam(new_model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
    
    batch_size = 10  # number of synthetic textures
    textures = []
    ground_truth = []  # simulated psychophysical thresholds (e.g., normalized average luminance)
    
    for _ in range(batch_size):
        tex = generate_texture(128, 128, imbalance_factor=0.3)
        textures.append(tex)
        gt_val = np.mean(tex) / 255.0  # normalized average intensity as a simulated threshold
        ground_truth.append(gt_val)
    
    base_outputs = []
    new_outputs = []
    
    # Evaluate models on each texture
    for i, (img, gt) in enumerate(zip(textures, ground_truth)):
        tensor_in = prepare_tensor(img).to(device)
        
        # Forward pass Base Method
        pred_base = base_model(tensor_in)
        base_outputs.append(pred_base.item())
        
        # Forward pass New Method
        pred_new = new_model(tensor_in)
        new_outputs.append(pred_new.item())
        
        print(f"Texture {i+1}: Ground Truth = {gt:.4f}, Base Prediction = {pred_base.item():.4f}, New Prediction = {pred_new.item():.4f}")
    
    # Compute error metrics: mean absolute errors
    errors_base = np.abs(np.array(base_outputs) - np.array(ground_truth))
    errors_new = np.abs(np.array(new_outputs) - np.array(ground_truth))
    
    mae_base = np.mean(errors_base)
    mae_new = np.mean(errors_new)
    
    print(f"\nMean Absolute Error (Base Method): {mae_base:.4f}")
    print(f"Mean Absolute Error (New Method): {mae_new:.4f}")
    
    # Paired t-test between the two methods over textures
    t_stat, p_val = ttest_rel(errors_base, errors_new)
    print(f"Paired t-test: t-statistic = {t_stat:.4f}, p-value = {p_val:.4f}")
    
    # Plot error bars for both methods
    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
    plt.plot(range(1, batch_size+1), errors_base, 'o-', label="Base Method Error")
    plt.plot(range(1, batch_size+1), errors_new, 's-', label="New Method Error")
    plt.xlabel("Texture Sample Index")
    plt.ylabel("Absolute Error")
    plt.title("Error Comparison between Base and New Methods")
    plt.legend()
    plt.savefig("salience_error_comparison.pdf", bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.close()

###############################
# Experiment 2: Adaptive Frequency Visualization and Analysis
###############################
def experiment2_frequency_visualization(device):
    print("Running Experiment 2: Adaptive Frequency Visualization and Analysis")
    # Instantiate model and optimizer
    new_model = NewMethod(embedding_size=10).to(device)
    criterion = nn.MSELoss()
    optimizer_new = optim.Adam(new_model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
    
    # Create a controlled dataset: sine textures with known frequencies
    frequencies = [3, 5, 7, 10]
    sine_textures = [generate_sine_texture(128, 128, f) for f in frequencies]
    
    epochs = 20  # short training loop for demonstration
    for epoch in range(epochs):
        epoch_loss = 0.0
        for f, texture in zip(frequencies, sine_textures):
            tensor_in = prepare_tensor(texture).to(device)
            # Create a synthetic ground truth: use normalized average intensity plus a small function of log-frequency.
            gt_val = np.mean(texture) / 255.0 + 0.1 * np.log(f + 1)
            gt_threshold = torch.tensor([[gt_val]], dtype=torch.float32, device=device)
            
            optimizer_new.zero_grad()
            pred = new_model(tensor_in)
            loss = criterion(pred, gt_threshold)
            loss.backward()
            optimizer_new.step()
            epoch_loss += loss.item()
        avg_loss = epoch_loss / len(sine_textures)
        print(f"Epoch {epoch+1}/{epochs}, Loss: {avg_loss:.4f}")
    
    # After training, extract learned frequency parameters from the sinusoidal encoding layer
    learned_freqs = new_model.sinusoid.freqs.detach().cpu().numpy()
    # Plot histogram of learned frequencies
    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
    sns.histplot(learned_freqs.flatten(), bins=20, color="blue", label="Learned Frequencies", kde=False)
    plt.xlabel("Frequency Value")
    plt.ylabel("Count")
    plt.title("Distribution of Learned Sinusoidal Frequencies")
    plt.legend()
    plt.savefig("frequency_distribution_newmethod.pdf", bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.close()
    
    # For comparison, simulate fixed Fourier frequencies (evenly spaced across range)
    total_elements = learned_freqs.size
    fixed_fourier_freqs = np.linspace(0, 10, num=total_elements)
    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
    sns.histplot(fixed_fourier_freqs, bins=20, color="green", label="Fixed Fourier Frequencies", kde=False)
    plt.xlabel("Frequency Value")
    plt.ylabel("Count")
    plt.title("Distribution of Fixed Fourier Frequencies")
    plt.legend()
    plt.savefig("frequency_distribution_fixed_fourier.pdf", bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.close()

def experiment3_natural_image_test(device):
    print("Running Experiment 3: Natural Image Generalization Test")
    # Use torchvision transforms for image preprocessing
    preprocess = transforms.Compose([
        transforms.Resize((128, 128)),
        transforms.ToTensor()  # scales to [0, 1]
    ])
    
    # Load image paths from a directory (use BSDS500_images/ if available)
    image_dir = "BSDS500_images"
    image_paths = glob.glob(os.path.join(image_dir, "*.jpg"))
    
    if len(image_paths) == 0:
        print("No natural images found in 'BSDS500_images/' directory. Skipping Experiment 3.")
        return  # Skip experiment 3 if no images are available
    
    # Instantiate both models
    base_model = BaseMethod().to(device)
    new_model = NewMethod(embedding_size=10).to(device)
    
    # Set models to evaluation mode
    base_model.eval()
    new_model.eval()
    
    results = []
    
    def get_salience_map(model, image_tensor):
        # For demonstration, assume the network returns a scalar threshold.
        with torch.no_grad():
            output = model(image_tensor.unsqueeze(0))  # add batch dimension
        return output.item()
    
    for path in image_paths:
        try:
            image = Image.open(path).convert("L")  # convert to grayscale
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"Error loading image {path}: {e}")
            continue
        tensor_img = preprocess(image).to(device)
        
        # In a more extensive pipeline we would extract multi-scale patches.
        # For simplicity, we use the whole image as input.
        salience_base = get_salience_map(base_model, tensor_img)
        salience_new = get_salience_map(new_model, tensor_img)
        
        print(f"Image: {os.path.basename(path)} | Base Salience: {salience_base:.4f} | New Salience: {salience_new:.4f}")
        results.append((path, salience_base, salience_new))
    
    # Plot a bar chart comparing salience predictions across images
    indices = np.arange(len(results))
    base_preds = [r[1] for r in results]
    new_preds = [r[2] for r in results]
    
    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
    width = 0.35
    plt.bar(indices - width/2, base_preds, width, label="Base Method")
    plt.bar(indices + width/2, new_preds, width, label="New Method")
    plt.xlabel("Image Index")
    plt.ylabel("Predicted Salience")
    plt.title("Comparison of Salience Predictions on Natural Images")
    plt.legend()
    plt.savefig("natural_image_salience_comparison.pdf", bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.close()
    
    # (Optional) If ground truth is available (e.g., from psychophysical data), one could compute correlation metrics.
    print("Experiment 3 completed on natural images.")

def run_tests():
    """
    Runs a quick test of all three experiments. The test versions run minimal loops to quickly finish.
    """
    print("Starting tests for all experiments...")
    device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
    print(f"Using device: {device}")
    
    # Run Experiment 1 test
    experiment1_synthetic_texture_test(device)
    
    # Run Experiment 2 test
    experiment2_frequency_visualization(device)
    
    # Run Experiment 3 test (will execute only if images available)
    experiment3_natural_image_test(device)
    
    print("All experiments (tests) executed successfully.")

###############################
if __name__ == '__main__':
    run_tests()

2. Two model variants are defined: the BaseMethod and the NewMethod (which uses an adaptive sinusoidal encoding layer).
3. Experiment 1 creates synthetic textures, computes model outputs, calculates mean absolute errors for both models, performs a paired t-test, and saves a PDF plot illustrating sample-by-sample error.
4. Experiment 2 trains the New Method on sine textures (with known frequencies) for a few epochs. Then it plots and saves histograms comparing the learned sinusoidal frequencies with fixed Fourier frequencies.
5. Experiment 3 loads natural images from a specified directory (BSDS500_images) and compares the salience predictions of both models. A bar chart comparing predictions is saved as a PDF.
6. The run_tests() function calls all three experiments with settings to finish quickly so that you can easily verify execution.

Make sure to install all required Python libraries and place any necessary natural image dataset (if available) in a folder named "BSDS500_images" before running the experiment.
